new_statements.quote: un accent grave (¥) indique un accent automatique placé sur la syllabe antépénultième par une règle phonologique; dans les mots à une ou deux syllabes, cet accent grave placé sur la première syllabe est prononcé à l'état isolé du mot, mais si celui-ci est précédé par un particule ou autre mot dans la même phrase accentuelle, l'accent se déplace et il est prononcé sur la dernière syllabe du mot ou particule précédant. [...] un accent aigu (¥) au-dessus d'une voyelle (v) signale un accent lexical (dans un substantif ou autre mot qui n'est pas un verbe), un accent grammatical superposé (surtout pour les verbes « intensifs »), ou un accent en syllabe finale (surtout en dialecte Kal Ansar) [...]. Tous ces accents sont fixes, et se trouvent sur une syllabe finale ou pénultième
new_statements.translation: A grave accent indicates an automatic accent placed on the antepenultimate syllable by a phonological rule; in words of one or two syllables, this grave accent placed on the first syllable is pronounced when the word is in isolation, but if the word is preceded by a particle or another word in the same accentual phrase, the accent moves and is pronounced on the last syllable of the preceding word or particle. [...] An acute accent above a vowel signals a lexical accent (in a noun or other non-verb word), a superimposed grammatical accent (mainly for 'intensive' verbs), or a final-syllable accent (mainly in the Kal Ansar dialect) [...]. All these accents are fixed, and are found on a final or penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog stress on syllable 1 of 2, 1 of 3, 2 of 4, 3 of 5 encodes antepenultimate stress with initial stress in 1-2 syllable words; Heath's default accent is exactly that (antepenult; initial in mono- and disyllables in isolation). Heath adds (a) that the default accent is phrase-sensitive (in 1-2 syllable words it moves to the last syllable of the preceding word within an accentual phrase), (b) a layer of marked lexical/grammatical accents fixed on the final or penult in nouns/non-verbs and intensive verbs, (c) suffix/clitic-conditioned penult accent, (d) secondary accents preceding the main accent. Compatible default placement; the marked-accent layer is a lexical/morphological except…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (automatic) word accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable by phonological rule; in words of one or two syllables it falls on the initial syllable when the word is in isolation, but inside an accentual phrase it shifts to the final syllable of the preceding word or particle. Over this default sit marked accents that are fixed on the final or penult: lexical accents in nouns and other non-verbs, grammatical accents (chiefly intensive verb stems), final accents from resyllabification (chiefly Kal Ansar/T-ka), and a suffix/clitic-conditioned penult accent required by a fixed set of suffixes and clitics (e.g. feminine singular -t, possessor and imperative-plural suffixes). Heath states there is no phonetic difference between these accent types.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 7: 'Dans certaines phrases, des accents secondaires précèdent l'accent principal.' (In some phrases, secondary accents precede the main accent.) No rule for their placement is given in the dictionary.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically accented nouns/non-verbs (accent fixed on final or penult, e.g. ummáʔin 'tea equipment', á-myar 'old man'); grammatical accent on intensive verb stems (ə-ujój 'he is far'); final-syllable accent from resyllabification in Kal Ansar dialect (i-jól 'he went'); suffix- and clitic-conditioned penult accent (t-e-kanési-t-t 'hedgehog'; possessor suffixes, 2pl imperative suffixes, 1sg possessor, etc. are marked in entries as 'requires accent on preceding syllable'); when an automatic accent lands on the syllable already carrying a lexical accent only the automatic one is written (e-kánay sg. vs i-kănəy-ăn pl.). Dictionary also notes [X t-o..] entries where a noun's accent shifts onto the preceding word in an accentual phrase (p. 9).
new_statements.identity_note: Heath 2006 covers the Tamashek dialects of Mali (Timbuktu zone: Kal Ansar = T-ka, Imeddedeghan = T-md; Kidal zone: Kal Idnan = K-d; Gourma Rharous = R; Gourma near Ansongo = A-grm), explicitly excluding Tawellemmett of the Menaka area and Niger. The final-syllable accent from resyllabification is stated to be chiefly a Kal Ansar (T-ka) feature. The Avant-propos refers readers to Heath 2005, A Grammar of Tamashek (Tuareg of Mali), Mouton de Gruyter, for the full accent rules; that grammar was not in the works list and was not opened.

sources.quote: No word-accent/stress placement rule is given anywhere (all 'stress' hits are either emphasis/syntax or the stative vowel). Only: 'In the stative aspect of the verb, a vowel can be heavily stressed. It is longer than a standard long vowel and heavily accented' and 'The stative differs from the perfective only by the one vowel (or by the stress placed on one vowel)'. This corroborates Heath's grammatical accent formative in the Resultative ('stative') stem but says nothing about default antepenult accent or lexical noun accent.
